tagline: Twin peaks rising from the sea
overview:
Saint Lucia is a teardrop-shaped volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean, part of the chain of Lesser Antilles between Martinique to the north and Saint Vincent to the south. It is about 616 km², roughly three times the size of Washington, D.C., and almost entirely green and mountainous.

About 180,000 people live on the island. English is the official language, but most people also speak Kwéyòl, a French-based creole, at home. Castries, the capital, sits on a deep natural harbor on the northwest coast where cruise ships tie up beside the market.

Saint Lucia is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Bananas were once the main export and tourism now leads, drawn by the Pitons, two volcanic spires that rise straight out of the sea and appear on the national flag's home ground. For its size, Saint Lucia has produced a remarkable number of celebrated writers and thinkers.
landAndNature: The Pitons, Gros Piton and Petit Piton, are lava plugs that jut about 770 and 740 meters above the water near the town of Soufrière, and they are a World Heritage site. Nearby, the Sulphur Springs are billed as a drive-in volcano: a road runs into a collapsed crater where gray mud bubbles and steam hisses from vents. Rainforest covers the interior mountains, where the Saint Lucia parrot, a blue-faced green bird found nowhere else, was brought back from about 100 birds in the 1970s to over 1,000 today. Waterfalls drop into warm pools, mangroves line some bays, and reefs off the west coast draw divers. The island lies in the hurricane belt and has been battered more than once.
peopleAndCulture: Saint Lucian culture is a French-British-African mix, heard in Kwéyòl speech and tasted in green figs and saltfish, the national dish of boiled green bananas with salted cod. Jounen Kwéyòl each October celebrates creole language, food and dress across the villages. La Rose and La Marguerite are rival flower societies whose members parade in costume and sing on their own feast days, a tradition unique to the island. Saint Lucia Jazz draws musicians from around the world each May. Cricket is the main sport, and Darren Sammy captained the West Indies to two Twenty20 World Cups. The island has produced two Nobel laureates, the economist Arthur Lewis and the poet Derek Walcott, the highest number per person of any country.
history: Kalinago people settled the island, calling it Iouanalao, after displacing earlier Arawak settlers. Europeans found it hard to hold: the island changed hands between Britain and France about fourteen times, earning it the nickname Helen of the West Indies after Helen of Troy. French planters established sugar estates worked by enslaved Africans, and Britain took final control in 1814. Slavery was abolished in 1834. Bananas replaced sugar as the great crop in the 1900s, and boatloads of green fruit shipped to Britain each week. Saint Lucia gained self-government in 1967 and became fully independent on February 22, 1979, remaining in the Commonwealth. Much of its economy has since shifted from farming to tourism, with hotels along the calm western coast.
funFacts: Saint Lucia has produced two Nobel Prize winners, more per person than any other country in the world.
The island changed hands between Britain and France about fourteen times, so both flags flew over it repeatedly.
A road leads right into the crater of Sulphur Springs, advertised as the world's only drive-in volcano.
The Saint Lucia parrot, found nowhere else, recovered from roughly 100 birds in the 1970s after strict protection.
Gros Piton and Petit Piton are hardened plugs of lava left behind after softer volcanic rock eroded away.
